\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$r_1+r_2$}
\opt{B}{$r_2-r_1$}
\opt{C}{$\dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1+r_2}$}
\opt{D}{$\dfrac{2r_1r_2}{r_1+r_2}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P1-PHY-S2-Q06, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=1, qno=6, type=multi, subtopic={Bohr model}, answer={A,B,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: standard problem in this chapter, bohr model, apply the relevant results | steps: apply the relevant results; compute}]
According to Bohr model, point like electrons orbit point like nucleus at particular, fixed radii. In a particular such atom with a nucleus of charge $Q=1.6\times10^{-18}$ C initially one electron is in orbital 1 at radial distance $r_1=47.7$ \AA\ from nucleus. The orbital 2 is at a radial distance $r_2=84.8$\AA. The electric force on electron in orbital 1 is $F_1$ and that in orbital 2 is $F_2$. The KE of electron in orbital 1 is $K_1$ and in orbital 2 is $K_2$.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The ratio of $\dfrac{F_1}{F_2}$ is greater than 3}
\opt{B}{$9K_1=16K_2$}
\opt{C}{When electron does a transition from orbital 1 to 2 it absorbs energy equal to 0.66 eV}
\opt{D}{$K_1-K_2=0.66$ eV}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P1-PHY-S2-Q07, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=1, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={Radioactivity}, answer={A,B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: standard problem in this chapter, radioactivity, apply the relevant results | steps: apply the relevant results; compute}]
A radioactive isotope with decay constant $\lambda$, starts leaking from a nuclear reactor at $t=0$ with rate $R(t)$, where $R(t)=R_0\,(1-e^{-Kt})$. Initially there were no atoms present outside the reactor (at $t=0$).
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The number of radioactive atoms present outside the reactor at any time $t$ is $n(t)=R_0\left[\dfrac1\lambda\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)+\dfrac{1}{\lambda-K}\left(e^{-\lambda t}-e^{-Kt}\right)\right]$.}
\opt{B}{The number of radioactive atoms present outside the reactor after a long time is $n(t)=\dfrac{R_0}{\lambda}$.}
\opt{C}{The number of radioactive atoms present outside the reactor at any time $t$ is $n(t)=R_0\left[\dfrac{1}{\lambda-K}\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)+\dfrac{1}{\lambda-K}\left(e^{-\lambda t}-e^{-Kt}\right)\right]$.}
\opt{D}{The number of radioactive atoms present outside the reactor after a long time is $n(t)=\dfrac{R_0}{\lambda-K}$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\opt{B}{The first ionisation energy of this atom will be $\dfrac{41}{128}\dfrac{me^4}{h^2\epsilon_0^2}$}
\opt{C}{Taking the reference of potential energy at infinity as zero, the energy of an electron is negative of twice of kinetic energy.}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SI08-P1-PHY-S3-G5-6, source={Score-I - Test 08 (09 Feb 2022)}, questions={5-6}]
One important application of radioactivity is the determination of the age of archaeological or geological samples. If an object contains radioactive nuclei when it is formed, then the decay of these nuclei marks the passage of time like a clock, half of the nuclei disintegrating during each half-life. If the half-life is known, a measurement of the number of nuclei present today relative to the number present initially can give the age of the sample. The radiocarbon technique utilizes the $^{14}_{\ 6}$C isotope of carbon, which undergoes $\beta^-$ decay with a half-life of $2\times10^{11}$ sec. This isotope is present in the earth's atmosphere at an equilibrium concentration of about one atom for every $7\times10^{11}$ atoms of normal carbon $^{12}_{\ 6}$C. It is often assumed that this value has remained constant over the years because $^{14}_{\ 6}$C is created when cosmic rays interact with the earth's upper atmosphere, a production method that offsets the loss via $\beta^-$ decay. Moreover, nearly all living organisms ingest the equilibrium concentration of $^{14}_{\ 6}$C. However, once an organism dies, metabolism no longer sustains the input of $^{14}_{\ 6}$C, and $\beta$ decay causes half of the $^{14}_{\ 6}$C nuclei to disintegrate every $2\times10^{11}$ sec. Take $\ln 2=0.7$
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI09-P2-PHY-S1-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 09 (16 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=5, type=multi, subtopic={Nuclear physics}, answer={A,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: standard problem in this chapter, nuclear physics, apply the relevant results | steps: apply the relevant results; compute}]
A heavy nucleus $N$, at rest, undergoes fission $N\to P+Q$, where $P$ and $Q$ are two lighter nuclei. Let $\delta=M_N-M_P-M_Q$, where $M_P$, $M_Q$ and $M_N$ are the masses of $P$, $Q$ and $N$, respectively. $E_P$ and $E_Q$ are the kinetic energies of $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The speed of $P$ and $Q$ are $v_P$ and $v_Q$, respectively. If $c$ is the speed of light, which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct ?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$E_P+E_Q=c^2\delta$}
\opt{B}{$E_P=\left(\dfrac{M_P}{M_P+M_Q}\right)c^2\delta$}
\opt{C}{$\dfrac{v_P}{v_Q}=\dfrac{M_Q}{M_P}$}
\opt{D}{The magnitude of momentum for $P$ as well as $Q$ is $c\sqrt{2\mu\delta}$, where $\mu=\dfrac{M_PM_Q}{(M_P+M_Q)}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SII33-P2-PHY-S2-G7-8, source={Score-II - Test 33 (01 Apr 2024)}, questions={7-8}]
In a gas where rms thermal speed is $v_t\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{3kT}{m}}\right)$, coulomb force will ensure that two nuclei each with charge q, cannot approach each other any closer than the distance of closest approach $r_m$. The value of $r_m$ is the distance at which their kinetic energy is completely converted to potential energy. Separation between two hydrogen nuclei in core of the sun cannot be small enough to allow fusion to occur. Known temperature that exists in the sun's core, coulomb force will cause the nuclei to remain at distance from each other equal to 100-1000 (or more) of nuclear radii $\left(\simeq10^{-15}\text{m}\right)$. So according to classical physics proton fusion reaction should not occur in sun. But if we consider quantum nature of nuclei, quantum-mechanical tunneling allows the protons to go under the coulomb barrier with a good probability. Bridging criteria for fusion was found to be $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv_t}\leqslant r_m$ where $\lambda$ is the de Broglie wavelength of moving proton when it is at large distance from the other proton. Wherever this equation is satisfied, two nuclei can approach each other arbitrarily closely so that nuclear force can lead to fusion. We find that the rms thermal speed in core of star must exceed a critical value for fusion to occur.
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SII33-P2-PHY-S2-G11-12, source={Score-II - Test 33 (01 Apr 2024)}, questions={11-12}]
In a hydrogen atom, the electron revolves around the nucleus (proton) in circular path. In addition, then electron also spins about it's own axis. Due to this spin, electron has a magnetic dipole moment $(\vec\mu)$ in direction opposite to it's spin angular momentum $\left(\vec S\right)$. As seen from the frame of electron, the electron itself is only spinning, but the proton is moving around it in a circular path with the same speed and radius as electron in ground frame. This motion of proton around electron produces a magnetic field $\left(\vec B\right)$. This magnetic field and magnetic dipole moment of electron have a mutual potential energy. If orbital angular momentum $\left(\vec L\right)$ of electron and it's spin angular momentum $\left(\vec S\right)$ are parallel, the potential energy is different from the case when they are anti parallel.
\end{bankpassage}

\textbf{Paragraph for Questions 9 and 10}

Figure shows how the resistance of a resistor and the reactances of an inductor and a capacitor vary with angular frequency $\omega$. Resistance R is independent of frequency, while the reactances X$_L$ and X$_C$ are not. If $\omega=0$, corresponding to a dc circuit, there is no current through a capacitor because $X_C\to\infty$, and there is no inductive effect because $X_L=0$. In the limit $\omega\to\infty$, $X_L$ also approaches infinity, and the current through an inductor becomes vanishingly small; recall that the self-induced emf opposes rapid changes in current. In this same limit, $X_C$ and the voltage across a capacitor both approach zero.

Figure shows an application of the above discussion to a loudspeaker system. Low-frequency sounds are produced by the woofer, which is a speaker with large diameter; the tweeter, a speaker with smaller diameter, produces high frequency sounds. In order to route signals of different frequency to the appropriate speaker, the woofer and tweeter are connected in parallel across the amplifier output. The capacitor in the tweeter branch blocks the low-frequency components of sound but passes the higher frequencies; the inductor in the woofer branch does the opposite.

\begin{center}
\bfigi{172.3}{SII37_p1phy_q910_stem.png}
\end{center}
\end{bankq}

In a hypothetical atom, a negatively charged particle having a charge of magnitude $3e$ and mass $3m$ revolves around a proton. Here, $e$ is the electronic charge and $m$ is the electronic mass. Mass of proton may be assumed to be much larger than that of the negatively charged particle, thus the proton is at rest. This ``atom'' obeys Bohr's postulate of quantization of angular momentum, that is $mvr=n\left(\dfrac h{2\pi}\right)$. It is given that for the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen atom: radius of orbit is $r_0$, speed of electron is $V_0$, and total energy is $-E_0$. The momentum of an emitted photon when it makes a transition from the second excited state to ground state, is
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\dfrac{8E_0}c$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{E_0}c$}
\opt{C}{$\dfrac{24E_0}c$}
\opt{D}{None of these}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

If the energy of a molybdenum atoms with a K electron knocked out is 27.5 keV, the energy of this atom when an L electron is knocked out will be \underline{\hspace{1cm}} keV. (Round off to the nearest integer) [$h=4.14\times10^{-15}$ eVs, $c=3\times10^8$ ms$^{-1}$]
\end{bankq}

Moseley's law for $K_\alpha$ photon is given by $\sqrt\upsilon=a(Z-b)$ where $a$ is a universal constant and $b$ is a screening constant. Moseley's logic helps us assume $b=1$ for $K_\alpha$ photon. If there is a percentage error $=10^{-2}$ in the measurement of '$b$' due to actual orbital configuration of an atom, then the relative error in the measurement of $\upsilon$ if $Z=51$ is $p\times10^{-q}$. Then mark the correct options.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Value of $p$ is $=4$}
\opt{B}{Value of $p$ is $=3$}
\opt{C}{Value of $q$ is $=7$}
\opt{D}{Value of $q$ is $=6$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
